question: How long do I have to use my GI Bill? I got out in 2019.
redacted_question: How long do I have to use my GI Bill? I got out in 2019.
answer: Because your last discharge or release from active duty was on or after January 1, 2013, your Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits do not expire, and there is no 15-year time limit for you [D02]. Your profile shows a 2019 separation, so this applies to you. Keep in mind the benefit covers up to 36 months of education benefits [D01]. To confirm your own benefit percentage, apply for a Certificate of Eligibility [D01].

question: I left the Air Force in 2010. Does my GI Bill expire?
redacted_question: I left the Air Force in 2010. Does my GI Bill expire?
answer: Separation in 2010 is before January 1, 2013, so your Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits generally expire 15 years after your last period of active duty of at least 90 consecutive days [D02]. Since today is October 7, 2026, that 15-year mark falls in 2025 for a 2010 separation, meaning it may already have passed, though the exact month isn't in my information. Some exceptions apply, so confirm your end date with VA before making plans [D02]. You can check your benefit details by applying for a Certificate of Eligibility [D01].

question: I'm separating in about two months. Can I still do SkillBridge?
redacted_question: I'm separating in about two months. Can I still do SkillBridge?
answer: Probably yes, but timing matters. SkillBridge takes place during your last 180 days of service [D14]. With 69 days until your December 15, 2026 separation, you are inside that window now. You need your commander's approval and must have completed required transition steps first, and availability varies by branch and installation [D14]. Completing TAP builds your Individual Transition Plan, a prerequisite for SkillBridge [D13]. Contact your installation's transition office right away to see if there's still time and what's open to you [D13][D14].

question: Do I have to pay the VA funding fee on a home loan?
redacted_question: Do I have to pay the VA funding fee on a home loan?
answer: Probably not. Most VA home loan borrowers pay a one-time VA funding fee, but veterans who receive VA disability compensation are exempt from it [D10]. Your profile shows a 30% VA disability rating, so if you receive VA disability compensation, you would be exempt [D10]. To confirm your status, start by requesting a Certificate of Eligibility (COE) [D10]. Private lenders set interest rates and credit requirements, so compare offers from more than one lender [D10].

question: How do I check my claim status? I always used eBenefits.
redacted_question: How do I check my claim status? I always used eBenefits.
answer: To check your claim status, sign in to VA.gov and open your claim status page; you can also upload evidence there [D06]. question: I heard the GI Bill doesn't work for trade school. Is that true?
redacted_question: I heard the GI Bill doesn't work for trade school. Is that true?
answer: No, that isn't accurate. Depending on the benefit you're eligible for, GI Bill education benefits can cover vocational and technical training, non-college degree programs, apprenticeships and on-the-job training, licensing and certification tests, and flight training [D21]. The catch is that the school or program must be approved for VA benefits. You can use the VA GI Bill Comparison Tool to check whether a specific school or program is approved and what you can expect to receive [D21]. Do you know which GI Bill benefit you're eligible for? Your Certificate of Eligibility confirms your benefit level [D01].

question: I was in Iraq in 2007 around burn pits. Can I get VA health care?
redacted_question: I was in Iraq in 2007 around burn pits. Can I get VA health care?
answer: Probably worth applying. Most veterans discharged under conditions other than dishonorable can apply for VA health care, and your honorable discharge fits that [D08]. Veterans who served in locations with certain toxic exposures may also qualify under expanded eligibility rules from the PACT Act [D08]. Iraq is a listed location for possible burn pit exposure [D09]. You can use the VA.gov screening tools to check eligibility, and you can apply at any time online at VA.gov, by phone, by mail, or in person at a VA medical center [D09][D08]. VA makes the final eligibility decision [D09].

question: Can I transfer my GI Bill to my daughter? I separated in 2024.
redacted_question: Can I transfer my GI Bill to my daughter? I separated in 2024.
answer: Probably not, based on the sources. Transfers of Post-9/11 GI Bill benefits to a spouse or children must be requested while you are still serving, through the Department of Defense (milConnect), and you cannot request a transfer after you have separated or retired [D04]. Since you separated in 2024, the sources indicate the transfer window has closed. Your daughter may still be able to use other benefits, such as Dependents' Educational Assistance (DEA), which VA determines based on the veteran's service-connected disability status; apply through VA.gov [D24]. A VA-accredited representative can help you confirm your options.
